summary: Defines a new challenge type for ACME, the protocol certificate authorities use to automate certificate issuance. The challenge proves control of a domain by answering a special TLS handshake that uses ALPN, so validation can happen on the TLS port without needing HTTP or DNS changes.

eli5.summary: To prove you own a house, you answer a special knock on the front door. Here, a website proves it owns its name by answering a special secure-connection request.

questions: what is the acme tls-alpn challenge
how to validate a domain over tls for acme
what is the acme tls-alpn-01 challenge
why was the tls sni challenge replaced
subtitle: A way for a certificate authority to check domain ownership using nothing but a special TLS handshake on port 443.

tldr.problem: ACME could validate domain control over HTTP and DNS, but hosting providers, CDNs and TLS-terminating load balancers wanted to do it at the TLS layer without touching their backends' HTTP handling.
tldr.mechanism: The ACME client serves a self-signed certificate carrying the SHA-256 digest of the key authorization in a critical acmeIdentifier extension, and the ACME server connects on TCP port 443 offering only the ALPN protocol acme-tls/1 to check it.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the earlier TLS SNI challenge, which let users of some service providers claim other users' names. It is an opt-in method that providers must deliberately implement.

today: RFC 8737 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2020, and neither obsoleted nor updated by another RFC according to the unit metadata. It works with ACME as defined in RFC 8555.

sections.title: Why a TLS-Only Challenge
sections.content:
The Automatic Certificate Management Environment (ACME, RFC 8555) already describes ways to prove control of a domain name over HTTP and DNS. Deployment experience showed it is also useful to validate control using the TLS layer alone.

This helps hosting providers, Content Distribution Networks (CDNs) and TLS-terminating load balancers, because they can validate a domain without modifying the HTTP handling behavior of their backends.

The new challenge type is called tls-alpn-01. It needs a new application-layer protocol negotiated with the ALPN extension (RFC 7301). Since there is no existing deployment base, providers must change their software to support it, which makes it explicitly opt-in. Because providers must write new code anyway, the RFC can demand stronger controls in that code.
sections.eli5: Some companies answer the door for many houses at once. This gives them a way to prove a name is theirs without bothering the people inside.

sections.title: The tls-alpn-01 Challenge Object and Certificate
sections.content:
The challenge object has two fields: type, which is the string tls-alpn-01, and token, a random value that uniquely identifies the challenge. The token MUST have at least 128 bits of entropy, MUST use only the base64url alphabet, and MUST have trailing = padding stripped.

To prepare, the client builds a self-signed certificate. It MUST contain a subjectAlternativeName extension with a single dNSName entry holding the domain being validated, and an acmeIdentifier extension holding the SHA-256 digest of the challenge's key authorization. The acmeIdentifier extension MUST be critical, so that non-ACME software does not accidentally use the certificate.

The extension is identified by the object identifier id-pe-acmeIdentifier, defined as { id-pe 31 }. Its value is the DER encoding of Authorization ::= OCTET STRING (SIZE (32)).

The certificate MUST be provisioned so that it is returned in a TLS handshake where acme-tls/1 has been negotiated and a Server Name Indication (SNI) extension names the domain being validated.
sections.eli5: You write a secret code on a card, put the card in an envelope marked with your house name, and keep it ready. Only someone who knows the secret can make that exact card.

sections.title: How the ACME Server Validates
sections.content:
The client signals readiness by POSTing an empty JSON object ({}) to the challenge URL. The server then builds and stores the key authorization from the token and the client's account key.

Validation follows these steps:

  • The server computes the expected SHA-256 digest of the key authorization.
  • It resolves the domain name and picks one of the returned IP addresses (it MAY validate against several).
  • It opens a TLS connection to that address. The connection MUST use TCP port 443, and the server MUST offer an ALPN extension with the single protocol name acme-tls/1 and an SNI extension containing only the domain name.
  • It checks that acme-tls/1 was negotiated (and that the ALPN extension held only that value), and that the certificate has a subjectAltName with the validated dNSName and no other entries, plus a critical acmeIdentifier with the expected digest.

dNSName comparison MUST be case insensitive. Because ACME does not support Unicode identifiers, all dNSNames MUST be encoded using the Punycode rules of RFC 3492. If every check passes, validation succeeds; otherwise it fails.
sections.eli5: The inspector knocks on the door with a special knock, asks to see the card, and checks that the name and the secret code both match exactly. Any mismatch and the answer is no.

sections.title: The acme-tls/1 Protocol
sections.content:
The acme-tls/1 protocol MUST only be used for validating ACME tls-alpn-01 challenges. It is just a TLS handshake that carries the validation information. It carries no application data: once the handshake is done, the client MUST NOT exchange any further data and MUST immediately close the connection.

Although it uses X.509 certificates, it does not use the authentication method of RFC 5280. It does not need a valid signature on the certificate, nor does it need the handshake to complete successfully. Since an ACME server may want to use an off-the-shelf TLS stack that cannot easily allow this, the server MAY withhold authorization if the certificate signature is invalid or the handshake does not fully complete.

ACME servers that implement it MUST only negotiate TLS 1.2 or higher when connecting to clients for validation.
sections.eli5: This special knock is only for proving who you are. Once the inspector has looked at your card, the conversation ends right away and nothing else is said.

sections.title: Security Assumptions
sections.content:
The design relies on assumptions about how an HTTPS server behaves during validation. First, a server that hosts many DNS names on one IP address must keep control of those names separate. If User A owns Host A and User B owns Host B, then a request with SNI for Host A must not be answered by User B, or User B could illegitimately validate control of Host A.

Second, a server must not violate RFC 7301 by blindly agreeing to use acme-tls/1 without understanding it.

To reduce the risk of users claiming each other's names, hosting providers, CDNs and other service providers SHOULD NOT allow users to supply their own certificates for TLS ALPN validation. If they implement it, they SHOULD generate the validation certificates themselves and not expose this to users. The RFC builds on the threat model in Section 10.1 of RFC 8555.
sections.eli5: If a building has many tenants, the doorman must only let each tenant answer for their own apartment. Otherwise someone could pretend to own a neighbor's door.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC records three registry entries:

  • In the SMI Security for PKIX Certificate Extension table, decimal 31 is id-pe-acmeIdentifier.
  • In the TLS ALPN Protocol IDs table, acme-tls/1 is registered with the identification sequence 0x61 0x63 0x6d 0x65 0x2d 0x74 0x6c 0x73 0x2f 0x31.
  • In the ACME Validation Methods registry, label tls-alpn-01 is registered for identifier type dns, usable with ACME.
sections.eli5: The RFC adds the new name, the new knock and the new method to the official lists so everyone uses the same ones.

sections.title: Why It Replaced the TLS SNI Challenge
sections.content:
This challenge exists to iterate on the TLS SNI challenge from the early ACME drafts. That challenge was convenient for providers operating large TLS-layer load balancers or servers fronting many DNS names, because validation stayed in the TLS layer.

A security issue discovered by Frans Rosen let users of various service providers illegitimately validate control of other users' DNS names. The old design assumed a user could only answer SNI requests for names they had registered with the provider, but a number of large providers did not honor that. The SNI name used was a subdomain of the validated name, so it was likely not already registered with the provider, which made a hijack much easier. The value of the method was still considered large enough to write this replacement.
sections.eli5: The old secret knock had a flaw: sneaky neighbors could answer it for houses that were not theirs. The new knock fixes that.
